pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Scientific Name Mycosphaerella coffeicola ; this is the name of the sexual form of the fungus; the disease is also known by the asexual form, Cercospora coffeicola .

type_of_disease.quote: this is the name of the sexual form of the fungus; the disease is also known by the asexual form, Cercospora coffeicola

affected_parts.quote: Small brown spots occur on the leaves, more obvious on the upper surface ... On the berries, the infections are smaller than on leaves ... In nurseries, it can cause leaf fall of seedlings and, in severe cases, stem dieback.

summary.value: Small brown circular spots on leaves up to 15 mm diameter with light brown or grey centres, dark brown rings, and yellow margins; on berries, smaller irregular brown spots mainly on sun-exposed side.
summary.quote: Small brown spots occur on the leaves, more obvious on the upper surface. The spots can grow up to 15 mm diameter; they have light brown or sometimes light grey centres, surrounded by a wide, dark brown ring, and a yellow margin

diagnostic_features.value: Circular spots with bright grey centres, dark brown ring border, and yellow haloes on leaves; spots occur mostly between the veins; spore masses visible in grey centres; on berries spots are irregular, brown, and mainly on the sun-exposed side.
diagnostic_features.quote: Circular brown spots, mostly 5-10 mm, with bright grey centres and yellow haloes, typical of brown-eye leaf spot, Cercospora coffeicola. Spores of the fungus form in the grey centres

conflicts.note: Mycosphaerella coffeicola is the sexual (teleomorph) form; Cercospora coffeicola is the asexual (anamorph) form. Both names are used; no NCBI/MycoBank validation was available to confirm current accepted name.

type_of_disease.quote: White thread-like strands of the fungus, Pellicularia koleroga, on the underside of coffee leaves.

affected_parts.quote: The fungus forms mats and threads of light-coloured growth on the underside of leaves and twigs

summary.value: The fungus forms mats and threads of light-coloured growth on the underside of leaves and twigs. Leaves appear light grey and dry at first, then blacken and fall; dead leaves are held in place by fungal threads. Dark brown or black decaying leaves, twigs and berries; defoliation and fruit drop observed.
summary.quote: The fungus forms mats and threads of light-coloured growth on the underside of leaves and twigs (Photo 1). At first, the leaves appear light grey and dry. Later, the leaves blacken and fall. In severe cases the dead leaves become detached from the branches but are held in places by the threads of the fungus

diagnostic_features.value: White thread-like strands forming webs over the underside of leaves; black threads holding detached dead leaves on branches; mycelial threads (fungal strands) visible on twigs and petioles; sclerotia visible all over affected areas.
diagnostic_features.quote: Look for the white threads of the fungus forming webs over the underside of leaves, and causing leaf fall. Look for the black threads of the fungus that often hold the leaves in place.

look_alikes.quote: Compare with other thread blights, e.g., white thread blight, Marasmiellus ( Marasmius ) scandens ( see Fact Sheet no. 15 ), and horse hair blight, Marasmius crinis-equi

conflicts.note: TNAU lists Corticium salmonicolor as the causal agent of 'black rot or koleroga', while the Lucid Pacific Pests fact sheet lists Pellicularia koleroga for the same disease (also called koleroga/thread blight/black rot). These may refer to the same or overlapping disease complex; no taxonomy validation available to resolve.
TNAU uses 'Black rot or koleroga'; Lucid fact sheet uses 'Thread blight, koleroga disease, black rot' as common names for the same disease.

conflicts.canonical_value: Fungal mats and white threads on undersides of leaves and twigs; leaves grey then black and falling, held by fungal threads.
conflicts.alternative_value: Dark brown or black decaying leaves, twigs and berries; defoliation and fruit drop.
conflicts.note: TNAU describes predominantly black/dark brown decay and defoliation; Lucid describes the white-to-black thread progression more specifically.

affected_parts.quote: mines are formed and later develop over a large surface area leading to large necrotic patches. The larvae are present in the mines and feed on the mesophyll. Leaves become impaired

summary.value: Irregular brown spots on the upper leaf surface, pale yellow trails (mines) under the leaf epidermis, and large necrotic patches caused by larval mining.
summary.quote: Occurrence of irregular brown spots on the upper leaf surface. Appearance of pale yellow trails under coffee leaf epidermis. Presence of large necrotic patches.

diagnostic_features.value: Pale yellow trails (mines) visible under the leaf epidermis that develop into large necrotic patches; larvae present in the mines feeding on the mesophyll; irregular brown spots on the upper leaf surface.
diagnostic_features.quote: Initially, mines are formed and later develop over a large surface area leading to large necrotic patches. The larvae are present in the mines and feed on the mesophyll.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Coffee leaf rust, Hemileia vastatrix , was first described in 1869

type_of_disease.quote: Fungal spores germinate on the underside of the leaves and penetrate through the stoma

affected_parts.quote: irregular shaped spots on upper leaf surfaces. They are connected with yellow to orange powdery lesions (diseased tissue) on the lower leaf surfaces where the spores are located. ... Severe infestations may cause twigs to die back from the tips. Eventually entire trees can die.

summary.value: Irregular shaped spots on upper leaf surfaces connected with yellow to orange powdery lesions on the lower leaf surfaces where the spores are located. Leaves eventually dry up and turn brown. Infected trees may prematurely drop infected leaves resulting in long, bare branches. Large orange/yellow spots on the undersides of leaves lead to premature leaf fall.
summary.quote: The most noticeable symptoms of coffee rust are irregular shaped spots on upper leaf surfaces. They are connected with yellow to orange powdery lesions (diseased tissue) on the lower leaf surfaces where the spores are located. ... They eventually dry up and turn brown. ... Infected trees may prematurely drop infected leaves. This results in long, bare branches.

diagnostic_features.value: Yellow to orange powdery lesions on the lower leaf surface containing rust spores (uredinia erupting through stomata); spots mostly begin at leaf edges or tips where water collects; first lesions appear on lowermost leaves and infection progresses upward into the tree.
diagnostic_features.quote: Spots mostly begin to form at the leaf edges or tips where water collects. The first lesions usually appear on the lowermost leaves. The infection slowly progresses up into the tree.

conflicts.note: NCIPMC only mentions foliar symptoms; bioprotectionportal additionally notes twig dieback and whole-tree death in severe cases.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: In Brazil, the etiological agents of phoma spot are fungi Phoma tarda (RB Stewart) H. Verm. and Phoma costarricensis Echandi, 1957 (Pleosporales: Didymellaceae).

type_of_disease.quote: The phoma stain, Phoma spp., is a fungal disease that occurs in several countries around the world where coffee is grown

affected_parts.quote: the fungus attacks leaves, flowers, fruits and branches of the coffee plant, producing very characteristic lesions

summary.value: Produces circular dark-colored spots of varying sizes on leaves (up to 2 cm diameter), dark depressed lesions on branches (dry shoots), and necrosis of flowers and fruits. Leaves may curve and crack at edges.
summary.quote: On the leaves of the second and subsequent pairs of leaves, the disease produces circular spots of dark color and varying sizes, which can reach 2 cm in diameter

diagnostic_features.value: Circular dark-colored spots of varying sizes on leaves up to 2 cm in diameter; dark depressed lesions on branches that can involve the entire diameter (dry shoots); infection begins at the apical part in the terminal shoot and tender leaves; leaves curve and may present cracks when lesions reach edges.
diagnostic_features.quote: In the affected branches, a symptom also called dry shoots (Fig. 3), dark depressed lesions are seen, which can involve the entire diameter. On the leaves of the second and subsequent pairs of leaves, the disease produces circular spots of dark color and varying sizes, which can reach 2 cm in diameter

look_alikes.quote: When the lesions reach the edges of the leaves, they curve, may present cracks and the symptom can easily be confused with boron deficiency
